personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Hagrid is warm, exuberant, fiercely loyal, and emotionally transparent — he cries openly, brags proudly, and speaks in a distinctive working-class dialect with dropped consonants and idiosyncratic grammar. He is also stubbornly naive about dangerous creatures (Aragog, Grawp) and shows a recurring pattern of accidentally revealing information he shouldn't (the Snape/Dumbledore argument, foreshadowing about the Philosopher's Stone in earlier books). He can be hurt and sulky when his feelings are wounded (ignoring the trio after they drop his class), but responds immediately to directness and warmth. He is also capable of forceful authority ('I'm a teacher, Potter!') and physical courage, acting instinctively in a crisis. His voice is immediately recognizable: long, breathless sentences broken by dialect, emotional interjections, self-contradictions mid-sentence.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves Hagrid's dialect, warmth, and emotional transparency almost intact. His grief over Aragog is rendered faithfully — the handkerchief, the crying, the proud remembrance ('wish yeh coulda seen 'im in 'is prime'). His instinctive authority at the Katie Bell scene ('Get back! All o' yeh!') and his physical tenderness in calming her are well-executed. His naivety about dangerous creatures is retained through the Aragog subplot. His Hogsmeade appearance with the Stinksap bag is brief but characteristically cheerful. His reaction to Dumbledore's death — first disbelief, then inconsolable grief — matches the books closely.
personality_voice.difference: Two losses are notable. First, the sulking/reconciliation arc with the trio (book scenes 55–79) — in which Hagrid ignores them for weeks, they have to force their way into his hut, and the emotional confrontation re-establishes the relationship — is entirely absent from the film. This removes a display of his emotional sensitivity, his capacity for wounded pride, and his eventual warmth once disarmed. Second, the Snape/Dumbledore conversation he accidentally overheard (book scenes 123–135) — in which he reveals information he clearly knows he shouldn't, grows increasingly panicked and guilty, then tries to deflect — is entirely absent. This is a recurring book trait (Hagrid inadvertently disclosing secrets) that is lost. His confrontation with Filch (book scenes 138–141) — showing his assertive, slightly offended authority as a teacher — is also absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality traits — warmth, dialect, loyalty, emotional openness, creature love, naivety, instinctive courage — are preserved in what the film does show. The losses are real but concern secondary behavioral patterns (wounded pride, secret-leaking, assertive dignity) rather than the dominant characterization. A moderate deduction is warranted for the missing behavioral texture, but the main voice is strongly preserved.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In HBP, Hagrid serves multiple narrative functions: (1) security escort for Harry to Diagon Alley; (2) Care of Magical Creatures teacher with an active subplot around Aragog's illness and death; (3) an inadvertent intelligence source (the Snape/Dumbledore argument); (4) a key participant in the Felix Felicis / Slughorn memory sequence, as his grief and home provide the setting and emotional pretext that enables Harry to extract the memory; (5) an active combatant during the Death Eater attack, fighting off a Death Eater and surviving Hagrid's Hut being set ablaze; (6) a witness and bearer of Dumbledore's body; (7) a participant in the post-death staff meeting, where he is specifically consulted, defends Dumbledore, and argues for Hogwarts to remain open. He initiates, decides, and acts meaningfully across all these functions.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film retains: the Aragog subplot and the burial scene as the setting for the Slughorn memory extraction; the Death Eater attack (he survives, hut burns, he rescues Fang implicitly); the scene with Dumbledore's body (he stops short, shattered); the Hogsmeade/Stinksap scene as minor color. The film loses: the Diagon Alley escort and security role; the Snape/Dumbledore intelligence leak; the reconciliation visit to his hut; the full staff meeting where he argues to keep Hogwarts open and defends Dumbledore's burial wishes; his role in physically carrying Dumbledore's body to the funeral (book scene 307–308); his presence at the funeral beside Grawp (book scene 309–312).
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most significant agency loss is the staff meeting sequence. In the books, Hagrid is explicitly consulted, gives his view ('Well, I'm stayin'... It's me home'), defends Dumbledore against procedural minimization ('No other headmaster or headmistress gave more to this school'), and assents to Dumbledore's burial at Hogwarts. This is active participation in a major post-death decision. It is entirely absent from the film. His role in carrying Dumbledore's body at the funeral — a charged act of honor and grief — is also absent. The Diagon Alley escort role is absent. The intelligence-leak scene is absent. What remains in the film is largely reactive: he appears, grieves, survives. The Felix Felicis scene retains his passive but essential function as grief-provider and setting-anchor, which is the most important single narrative beat, and it is preserved.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Multiple agency losses across different narrative functions: the staff meeting (active voice in institutional decision), the funeral procession (honored bearer), the Diagon Alley escort (active protective role), the Snape intelligence (inadvertent plot contribution). The Felix Felicis scene — his single most narratively important appearance — is preserved. This is a substantial but not total agency reduction; he is not decorative, but he has lost meaningful participatory functions. Cap 3 (75) is implicated by the transfer/removal of his agency in the staff meeting and funeral, though these are not transferred to another character but simply removed.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Hagrid's motivations in HBP are relatively transparent: absolute loyalty to Dumbledore and Hogwarts; deep emotional attachment to creatures regardless of danger; protective love for Harry, Ron, and Hermione; and a persistent desire to be taken seriously as a teacher and trusted adult. His internal conflict in HBP is mild but present: he is torn between his genuine hurt at the trio dropping his class and his inability to stay angry at them for long. He also experiences tension between his knowledge of the Snape/Dumbledore argument and his instinct to protect Dumbledore's confidence — he knows he shouldn't have heard it and shouldn't be repeating it, yet Harry's pressure extracts it. His grief over Aragog is uncomplicated but deeply felt.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves his loyalty to Dumbledore (the devastation at his death is authentic), his creature attachment (Aragog grief is fully rendered), and his protectiveness toward Harry (the attack scene). The hurt at being dropped by the trio and the brief internal conflict over revealing the Snape argument are both absent, as those scenes are cut entirely.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The wounded-pride/reconciliation conflict is absent. The Snape intelligence tension is absent. What remains is the simpler motivational core: love, loyalty, grief.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The dominant motivations are intact. What is lost is a secondary layer of internal conflict — the pride/hurt tension and the secret-keeping tension — that adds texture but is not the defining motivational substrate. The simplification is real but not severe enough to misrepresent why Hagrid acts as he does in the film.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on cut scenes

character_arc.book_baseline: Hagrid's arc in HBP is not a transformation arc but an emotional endurance arc: he begins the year proud and hopeful (Grawp improving, Witherwings/Buckbeak happy, new term starting), suffers personal grief (Aragog's death), experiences institutional anxiety (worry about Hogwarts closing due to attacks), and ends the book in profound grief at Dumbledore's death, yet commits to staying at Hogwarts ('It's me home'). His final act is to carry Dumbledore's body — a gesture of honor that closes his arc with dignity despite loss. His arc is flat in terms of character change but emotionally meaningful as a through-line of loyalty tested by loss.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film captures the Aragog grief and the Dumbledore death grief. It omits the institutional anxiety subplot (worry about Hogwarts closing), the reconciliation arc, and the staff meeting resolution ('I'm stayin'). The funeral procession is absent. The film's Hagrid ends the story weeping and stopped short at Dumbledore's body, which is emotionally authentic but incomplete — the resolution of commitment ('It's me home') is missing.
character_arc.difference: The arc's emotional beats are partially present (grief over Aragog, grief over Dumbledore), but the institutional dimension and the resolving commitment beat are absent. The arc ends in grief without the affirmative close that the books provide.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed rather than falsified; the remaining emotional through-line is faithful. But the absence of the resolution beat (committing to stay, defending Hogwarts) means the arc is incomplete rather than merely compressed. A moderate deduction is appropriate.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent

key_relationships.book_baseline: Hagrid's three key relationships in HBP are: (1) Harry/trio — warm, protective, somewhat childlike mutual affection, occasionally strained (the dropping of his class causes real hurt); (2) Dumbledore — absolute loyalty, near-reverence, Dumbledore reciprocates by consulting and defending Hagrid; (3) Aragog — a relationship the books treat as one of Hagrid's defining irrationalities, an emotional bond with a creature that nearly killed his friends, presented with a mixture of pathos and comedy. A secondary relationship with Slughorn is briefly established at the burial.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Aragog relationship is well-rendered: grief, pride, burial. The Dumbledore relationship is captured in the death reaction — disbelief, inconsolable grief, stopping short at the body. The Harry/trio relationship is present but flattened: the estrangement, reconciliation, and the 'I'm a teacher, Potter!' assertive dignity scene are all absent. The Slughorn relationship is present and reasonably faithful.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry/trio relationship loses its most complex moment in HBP — the estrangement and reconciliation, which showed both Hagrid's emotional vulnerability and the genuine affection underlying the relationship. The Dumbledore relationship loses the staff meeting dimension, where Dumbledore's trust in Hagrid's views is explicitly confirmed by McGonagall and Hagrid responds with dignified grief and commitment. What remains is grief without the relational architecture that gives it full meaning.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The emotional core of the Hagrid/Harry relationship is recognizable but missing its most textured scene. The Dumbledore relationship is emotionally present but stripped of its reciprocal-institutional dimension. These are meaningful losses but not total ones; the dominant dynamics are still readable.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The book's Hagrid in HBP is rich with contradictions and texture: a powerful man reduced to sobbing over a spider his friends once fled for their lives; a teacher who sulks like a child when his students drop his class; an adult who accidentally leaks sensitive information he was sworn not to share; a man of deep physical courage who also needs emotional reassurance; someone who defends Dumbledore's legacy in a formal staff meeting with quiet dignity. He is simultaneously comic (Grawp as assistant, rock cakes, the Aragog eulogy) and genuinely moving (carrying Dumbledore's body, 'It's me home'). The tension between his naivety and his genuine emotional intelligence is a recurring source of complexity.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the Aragog grief/comedy tension well. The physical courage in the Death Eater attack is present. The speech patterns and emotional warmth are intact. What is lost: the wounded pride/reconciliation arc (complexity of his relationship with the trio), the Snape intelligence leak (his irresistible compulsion to share dangerous information), the staff meeting (his dignity and institutional loyalty), the funeral procession (his honored role), and the full Grawp subplot color (his optimistic delusion about Grawp as assistant).
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film retains the broad strokes — loyal, warm, creature-obsessed, emotionally transparent — but removes the scenes that make him contradictory and surprising: the teacher who sulks, the secret-keeper who can't keep secrets, the man whose grief council is formally sought by the acting headmistress, the bearer of the greatest wizard's body. What remains is a simpler, warmer, less conflicted Hagrid.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a meaningful simplification. The lost material is not cosmetic — the reconciliation scene, the Snape leak, and the staff meeting are each distinct facets of complexity that do not appear elsewhere in the film's Hagrid. The character is recognizable but substantially reduced in nuance. Cap 1 (85) is implicated. The score reflects significant but not catastrophic simplification.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for losses; directly evidenced for what is retained

lost_or_transferred_material: Diagon Alley security escort role (Book 6, Chapters 6–7): Hagrid's proud, bumbling protective function entirely absent from the film
Trio-drops-his-class estrangement arc: weeks of Hagrid ignoring the trio, his hurt pride, the forced reconciliation at his hut ('I'm a teacher, Potter!'), and his eventual forgiveness

Snape/Dumbledore argument intelligence leak: Hagrid inadvertently revealing a heated argument between Dumbledore and Snape, panicking when pressed, trying to deflect — a defining recurring trait (secret-leaking) entirely absent
Hagrid's confrontation with Filch outside the castle: assertive teacher dignity ('I'm a ruddy teacher, aren't I, yeh sneakin' Squib!') removed
Aragog funeral note and trio's debate about attending: Hagrid's written plea ('I can't face it alone') and the emotional weight of the request absent

Full Aragog burial scene texture: in the books, Slughorn covertly extracts venom while Hagrid is distracted; Hagrid drunkenly gives away the unicorn hair; the extended toasting sequence; Hagrid's emotional reminiscence about his father and Harry's parents — the film compresses this significantly

Staff meeting after Dumbledore's death: Hagrid participates, is specifically consulted by McGonagall ('Professor Dumbledore always valued your views'), commits to staying ('It's me home'), and defends Dumbledore's right to be buried at Hogwarts ('No other headmaster or headmistress gave more to this school') — entirely absent from the film
Carrying Dumbledore's body to the funeral: Hagrid bears the body wrapped in purple velvet — a deeply charged act of honor — absent from the film
Hagrid seated beside Grawp at the funeral, Grawp patting Hagrid's head: a moment of pathos and dark comedy that closes the Grawp subplot for the film — absent
Grawp-as-assistant subplot: Hagrid's delusional optimism about training Grawp as his Care of Magical Creatures assistant is entirely absent from the film corpus

Hagrid's institutional anxiety about Hogwarts closing due to the attacks: his worry that the board of governors will shut the school, drawing a parallel to the Chamber of Secrets — absent from the film
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85 ceiling): the film removes a major part of Hagrid's complexity, agency, and narrative function — the staff meeting, the funeral procession, the reconciliation arc, and the Snape intelligence leak collectively represent substantial lost characterization. Score kept below 85.

Cap 3 (75 ceiling): Hagrid's agency in the staff meeting (initiating and voicing the decision to keep Hogwarts open, defending Dumbledore's burial rights) is removed rather than transferred. Combined with the funeral procession agency loss, this pushes the score toward the 75 cap. Final score of 72 reflects this constraint.
key_observations: The film's Hagrid is emotionally recognizable and vocally faithful — his warmth, dialect, creature-love, and grief are all well-rendered, and the Aragog burial scene (his single most important HBP appearance) is preserved with good fidelity. However, the adaptation removes a substantial layer of complexity: the estrangement/reconciliation arc with the trio, the Snape intelligence leak, the staff meeting participation, and the funeral procession together eliminate most of what makes book-Hagrid in HBP surprising, contradictory, and institutionally significant. What remains is a simpler, warmer, more passive Hagrid — recognizable as the character but missing the scenes that made him multidimensional. The 72 score reflects a portrayal that is faithful in surface and tone but meaningfully reduced in agency, nuance, and narrative function.
